articles.title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
articles.summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk showcased the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
articles.body:
A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.

"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.

Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.

But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.

articles.title: Blue Origin’s reusable New Glenn rocket lands successfully, but payload delivery fails
articles.summary: But it failed to deliver its space-based cell tower payload.
articles.body: Today’s launch of AST SpaceMobile’s satellite aboard Blue Origin’s reusable rocket was a partial success. The New Glenn first stage booster touched back down on a drone ship without incident, its second launch and landing, and officially giving Jeff Bezos a reusable launch vehicle to compete with SpaceX’s Falcon 9. Unfortunately for Blue Origin and AST SpaceMobile, the overall mission was less successful. The Bluebird 7 cell-tower-in-space was delivered to a lower orbit than expected by the second stage of the launch vehicle, and it will be destroyed. The Orlando Sentinel reports that the FAA announced Sunday night that New Glenn has been grounded, pending an investigation by Blue Origin. [Media: In a statement, AST said: > During the New Glenn 3 mission, BlueBird 7 was placed into a lower than planned orbit by the upper stage of the launch vehicle. While the satellite separated from the launch vehicle and powered on, the altitude is too low to sustain operations with its on-board thruster technology and will de-orbited. The cost of the satellite is expected to be recovered under the company’s insurance policy. > BlueBird 7 would have been AST SpaceMobile’s eighth deployed into low Earth orbit and is one of many planned for its space-based cellular broadband network. The company is currently in production through BlueBird 32, with BlueBird 8 to 10 expected to be ready to ship in approximately 30 days. Blue Origin’s tweet from Sunday morning says: > NG-3 Update: We have confirmed payload separation. AST SpaceMobile has confirmed the satellite has powered on. The payload was placed into an off-nominal orbit. We are currently assessing and will update when we have more detailed information. Bezos posted a video of the landing on X without comment. [Media: Update, April 20th: Added additional information from the FAA, AST, and Blue Origin.

articles.title: Meet Raji Doshi, the 12-year-old who won ‘America’s Top Young Scientist 2026’ and $25,000 for her algae and aragonite plan to reduce ocean acidification
articles.summary: Ocean acidification rarely makes headlines the way storms or heatwaves do, yet it quietly changes the chemistry that coral, shellfish and other sea
articles.body: Ocean acidification rarely makes headlines the way storms or heatwaves do, yet it quietly changes the chemistry that coral, shellfish and other sea creatures rely on. One twelve-year-old from Connecticut has decided to take it on. Raji Doshi, a seventh-grade student at Talcott Mountain Academy, designed a coastal solution that pairs algae with natural calcium buffers, and it earned her a place among the ten national finalists of the 2026 3M Young Scientist Challenge. This article explains how her idea works, why she created it, which invention she admires most, and what she hopes to build in the future. Her project reflects a growing effort to find practical, nature-based ways to protect marine ecosystems from the effects of changing ocean chemistry.How a durable algae and aragonite alkalinity system aims to lower ocean acidity and protect sea lifeAccording to Raji's finalist profile on the 3M Young Scientist Lab, she created an innovative coastal solution that uses algae and natural calcium buffers to lower ocean acidity and boost marine health. Her project title describes it as a novel, durable algae and aragonite alkalinity system designed to reduce ocean acidification driven by carbon dioxide. Aragonite is a form of calcium carbonate, the mineral that many shell-building marine animals depend on, so the approach targets the chemistry of seawater directly. Talcott Mountain Science Centre reports that a closely matching version of the project won first place in physical sciences for seventh-grade individual entries at the Connecticut Science and Engineering Fair in March 2026, along with an invitation to compete in the Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge.Why Raji Doshi entered the 3M Young Scientist Challenge to test her ocean acidification researchRaji told the 3M Young Scientist Lab that she entered the challenge because she wanted to do something real with her research. She explained that studying ocean acidification in a classroom is one thing, but the competition gave her a reason to design an experiment, collect real data and test whether her idea could withstand scrutiny. She also told the Lab that climate change feels urgent to her because oceans are absorbing carbon at a rate that is changing their chemistry in ways that affect billions of people. The challenge appealed to her, she said, because it rewards students who communicate science clearly and think about real-world impact, which is exactly what she tried to do. She wanted to work on something that mattered rather than something that would simply earn a grade.Autonomous underwater vehicles, Raji Doshi's favourite invention, and what they teach us about oceansAsked by the 3M Young Scientist Lab to name her favourite invention of the past one hundred years, Raji chose the autonomous underwater vehicle, pointing to systems developed by organisations such as Saildrone and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. She told the Lab that these vehicles, including carbon-neutral ocean drones from Saildrone, let scientists gather real-time data on ocean chemistry, acidity levels and carbon dioxide absorption in remote and challenging environments. That information is critical, she said, for understanding and addressing ocean acidification. She added that their ability to operate on their own for months at a time makes them game-changers for monitoring the health of the oceans. The choice mirrors the emphasis she placed on collecting real data in her own research, and it shows how she connects technology, measurement and conservation.From seventh grade researcher to future aerospace engineer: Raji Doshi on climate goals and teamworkLooking ahead, Raji told the 3M Young Scientist Lab that in fifteen years she hopes to be a National Aeronautics and Space Administration aerospace engineer designing systems that monitor ocean health and climate change from space. That ambition links her work on seawater chemistry to observation from orbit. She said her research taught her that the most significant climate breakthroughs happen when different fields work together, and she wants to build the tools that make that collaboration possible. Her profile on the Lab website also features her personal motto, i.e., "Work hard in silence, let your success make the noise." The same page introduces her mentor, Deborah Isabelle, a product engineering specialist in abrasives who develops new products in the 3M Automotive Aftermarket Division and chairs the company's Science Encouragement Program.How Raji Doshi won the America's Top Young Scientist title at the 3M Young Scientist Challenge finalAs reported by USA Today, Doshi was announced the winner during the award ceremony; she will receive the grand prize of $25,000, a contest trophy, and the title of "America's Top Young Scientist 2026," according to 3M's website. The ten finalists, aged eleven to fourteen, spent the summer with 3M scientist mentors before gathering at the 3M Innovation Centre in Saint Paul, Minnesota, for live challenges and final presentations to judges. William Brown, chairman and chief executive officer of 3M, told the public in the release that the challenge turns student curiosity, scientific thinking and mentorship into real solutions, while Brian Shaw, chief executive officer of Discovery Education, said the finalists prove you can be a scientist at any age.

articles.title: Tesla unveils car that can drive upside down and jump through the air
articles.summary: Tesla has unveiled an electric car that can drive upside down and use rocket-like thrusters to jump and turn mid-air.
articles.body:
Tesla unveils car that can drive upside down and jump through the air

Tesla has unveiled an electric sports car that can drive upside down and use rocket-like thrusters to jump and turn mid-air. Developed with Elon Musk’s SpaceX, it can reportedly accelerate to 97km/h in under a second. First promised in 2017, the car is now expected in 2028.

articles.title: Tesla Roadster 'voa' com propulsores de ar comprimido de foguetes | G1
articles.standfirst: Esportivo elétrico usa tanques especiais de ar comprimido e libera os gases por bocais. Sistema de sucção permite que Tesla escale as paredes e faça curvas "grudado" na pista.
articles.summary: Esportivo elétrico de Elon Musk comprime o ar e libera os gases por bocais. Sistema de sucção permite que Tesla escale as paredes e faça curvas "grudado" na pista
articles.body:
Tesla Roadster flutua na rampa — Foto: divulgação/Tesla

A Tesla mostrou, nesta quinta-feira (15), a nova geração do esportivo Roadster flutuando e dando piruetas no palco. O recurso, segundo a Tesla, será oferecido ao clientes no veículo de produção.

O modelo é o mais potente já criado pela empresa de Elon Musk e chega a 370 km/h.

A Tesla usa no Roadster um sistema de propulsão a gás comprimido, uma tecnologia de bocais e válvulas acionadas por componentes derivados do robô Optimus.

O recurso foi desenvolvido para permitir manobras extremas e até a capacidade de pairar no ar.

O mecanismo central da versão Thrust é composto por um tanque de alta pressão, com capacidade para 200 litros e resistência de até 10.000 PSI.

Para a variante Rocket, o assento do passageiro é removido para dar lugar a um reservatório expansível de 400 litros, totalizando 600 litros de gás comprimido armazenado no veículo.

O acionamento das válvulas de alta precisão é realizado por atuadores baseados na tecnologia do robô Optimus.

Ao serem acionados, esses propulsores liberam o gás pressurizado por meio de bocais localizados na traseira da carroceria.

O Tesla Roadster na versão Rocket tem força do empuxo comparável à de um jato de combate, segundo os engenheiros da marca.

A versão extrema Rocket conta com seis propulsores adicionais integrados à estrutura . O conjunto inclui um propulsor em cada canto do automóvel para fornecer empuxo vertical e dois propulsores posicionados na parte dianteira para o controle de guinada.

Esse recurso de engenharia foi projetado para permitir que o veículo execute manobras direcionais auxiliadas pelo ar e consiga pairar.

O sistema opera sem processo de combustão . O uso do recurso é voltado exclusivamente para ambientes fora de estradas públicas, pois a força do jato pode arremessar detritos contra pedestres e outros veículos em circulação.

Durante a apresentação do novo esportivo, a Tesla demonstrou que o Roadster também consegue ficar preso a uma parede sem cair . Para isso, um ventilador na base do veículo cria uma sucção que o mantém “grudado” à superfície.

Tesla Roadster "voa" — Foto: divulgação/Tesla

“Ele pode puxar até 2 Gs [equivalentes a duas vezes a pressão atmosférica no nível do mar] para fazer o carro dirigir de ponta-cabeça, e pegamos emprestadas algumas tecnologias da SpaceX para fazer o resto", revelou Lars Moravy, vice-presidente de engenharia de veículos na Tesla.

Elon Musk afirmou que o poder de sucção do novo carro não foi pensado para permitir que uma pessoa dirija de ponta-cabeça, mas para manter o veículo mais firme contra o solo e, assim, melhorar sua capacidade de fazer manobras em alta velocidade.

Além de voar e dirigir de ponta-cabeça, a segunda geração do Roadster segue o design minimalista já adotado pela Tesla em outros modelos já lançados. Por fora, são raros os detalhes coloridos ou cromados.

Por dentro, há espaço apenas para duas pessoas e o painel traz acabamento com uma única textura visual.

A Tesla não revelou a ficha técnica completa do novo carro, mas informou que:

Acelera de 0 a 100 km/h em menos de 1 segundo ;

Tem autonomia de 482,8 km com uma carga;

Os faróis estão escondidos na carroceria, o que melhora a aerodinâmica do veículo;

Para reduzir o peso, o novo Roadster utiliza uma liga de magnésio e titânio, além de fibra de carbono na carroceria.

O novo Roadster será vendido em três versões:

Performance: utiliza o sistema de ventilação para melhorar a dirigibilidade nas curvas;

Thrust , em versão limitada : adiciona saídas de ar comprimido na traseira, que ajudam o carro a acelerar de 0 a 100 km/h em menos de um segundo;

Rocket , ainda mais limitada e vendida apenas por convite : remove um dos dois assentos, acrescenta mais saídas de ar pelo veículo e é a versão capaz de flutuar.

A fabricação do Roadster será iniciada em 2028, porém ainda não existe informação oficial sobre o preço do supercarro.

Protótipo do novo Tesla Roadster foi mostrado em 2017 e não lembra em quase nada o carro mostrado em 2026. — Foto: Divulgação / Tesla

Novo Roadster foi prometido quase 10 anos atrás

O protótipo deste novo Roadster foi revelado em 2017 com preço de US$ 200 mil e previsão inicial de entregas para 2020. O valor de tabela não foi atualizado desde então, mas as reservas continuam ativas mediante pagamento de US$ 50 mil.

Em outubro de 2025, Elon Musk, CEO da Tesla, afirmou que o novo Roadster poderia "voar". A afirmação ocorreu durante entrevista ao podcast de Joe Rogan, na qual o executivo confirmou que o desenvolvimento do carro esportivo continuava em andamento.

Durante a conversa, Musk citou a frustração de não existirem carros voadores no mundo atual. O executivo completou dizendo que as pessoas deveriam ser capazes de comprar um.

O novo esportivo é fruto de uma colaboração entre a Tesla e a SpaceX, empresa de foguetes também liderada por Musk.

Roadster de 1ª geração passou perto de Marte

Tesla Roadster de 1ª geração no espaço — Foto: divulgação/Tesla

O feito aconteceu em 6 de fevereiro de 2018, quando o foguete acionou os 27 motores em seu primeiro voo, decolou da plataforma de lançamento 39A do Centro Espacial Kennedy, nos Estados Unidos, e levou uma única carga a bordo: o carro.

O segundo estágio foi ativado poucas horas após o lançamento e queimou combustível para colocar o Roadster em uma órbita heliocêntrica ao redor do Sol, cuja maior distância da estrela corresponde à órbita de Marte.

O objetivo do lançamento, segundo o empresário Elon Musk, diretor executivo e principal acionista da Tesla, era deixar o Roadster em órbita de Marte por "centenas de milhões de anos".

"Eu adoro a ideia de um carro navegando aparentemente sem parar pelo espaço e talvez sendo descoberto por uma raça alienígena milhões de anos no futuro", disse o empresário durante o lançamento.

O veículo se aproximou de Marte em novembro de 2018, e segue em um movimento elíptico de ida e volta para a Terra.

Lançado em 2008 e vendido até 2012, o primeiro Roadster foi o veículo elétrico pioneiro da empresa e utilizava o chassi do Lotus Elise. O projeto ajudou a mudar a visão do mundo sobre o que um carro elétrico poderia ser. Uma unidade até foi lançada ao espaço.

Desde então, a fabricante ficou conhecida pelos utilitários esportivos Model Y e Model X e pelos sedãs Model S e Model 3.

A revelação da nova geração acontece em um momento de mudança de foco da Tesla. A companhia tem transferido a prioridade da fabricação de carros para motoristas humanos em direção à robótica e tecnologias de direção autônoma guiadas por inteligência artificial.

Neste ano, a montadora parou de vender os modelos Model S e Model X para abrir espaço para a produção de seus robôs humanoides Optimus.

A empresa também lançou o Cybercab, um robô-táxi de dois lugares projetado sem controles manuais, como volante, pedais e retrovisores.

articles.title: Revealed! New Tesla Roadster Takes Flight and Does Barrel Rolls with the Help of SpaceX Thrusters
articles.summary: The Roadster prototype also hit 60 mph in less than one second, just like Elon promised.
articles.body:
UPDATE 10/15/26, 9:30 p.m. ET: This story has been updated with photos and info from tonight's reveal event at SpaceX's testing facility in McGregor, Texas.

Tesla and CEO Elon Musk have finally revealed the long-awaited follow-up to the brand's first production car, the Roadster. It's been a long time coming—nine years, in fact—since we saw the ambitious concept for the second-generation electric sports car, but during tonight's event, which was attended by a select group of fans, media, and investors as well as livestreamed on Musk's social media platform, X, the new Tesla Roadster was unveiled in spectacular fashion, with a prototype driving upside down and actually taking flight.

It's now obvious why the event needed to be held outdoors, as its debut featured an arching Hot Wheels-like structure that a Roadster prototype was able to drive up thanks to a fan system underneath the car that Tesla claims provides 2 g's of suction, allowing it to stick to the road. After driving up the towering structure, the prototype's thrusters, which were supplied by SpaceX and said to produce over 80 kilonewtons of force, allowed it to fly forward and do a barrel roll before they slowly helped it land safely on the ground in a cloud of white smoke.

"It can basically fly like a rocket," Musk told the crowd. "It can do, like, crazy gymnastics. Whatever you want." He also added, jokingly, "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car, but it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10."

Musk went on to say that the Roadster will be an actual car that's on the roads. Though it's also worth noting that he said, "I'm not sure it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions, but there will be such a car that someone can own." While the CEO didn't provide many specs or say how much the production car will cost, he did say that they will start building it in 2028, adding "actually" with a laugh.

During the event, the Roadster prototype was also shown doing multiple acceleration tests, with the help of its four rear-mounted thrusters. The first run to 60 mph was done in a claimed one second. When Musk was reminded that he had promised the car would hit the mile-per-minute mark in less than one second, the Roadster's second run was done in a claimed 0.81 second. Musk then said that they anticipate they'll be able to do even better than that. And if you're wondering whether this thing will need jet fuel to power its thrusters, fret not, as they're actually fed by ultra-high-pressure air tanks, which the car can recharge itself.

What about top speed? Well, Musk claims the new Roadster will do "over 230 mph," but he said they want to crack half the speed of sound (383 mph). Among Musk's other big claims during the event, he said, "It's going to crush every track record that has ever existed." He also said that, long term, the Roadster will be the only manually driven car that Tesla makes—implying that the rest of the company's fleet will eventually be autonomous.

There were also few details about the Roadster's interior, though we did get a short glimpse during the livestream, which showed the coupe's butterfly doors opening to reveal a two-seat cabin with a yoke-style steering wheel to the left of a large horizontally oriented screen.

Tesla says the Roadster's design was inspired by aircraft such as the SR-71 Blackbird, and the wedge-shaped super EV also has a striking resemblance to the white Lotus Esprit S1 that James Bond drove in The Spy Who Loved Me . While that famous movie car was able to turn into a submarine, it didn't have a large active rear wing like the Roadster prototype.

Now that we've seen it in person, we can tell that the deployed version was used in the reveal's teaser image, only it was upside down. Tesla says this trick rear wing has two modes—high drag and high downforce—and it can automatically adjust its pitch. The Roadster's fan system also has two modes: one that can suction the car to the ground at low speeds for increased traction, and another for high-speed performance that opens up the front and rear sections of the suction system to create even more flow underneath the car.

We should also point out that the prototype doing the stunts was different than the one that was driven on stage. The big giveaway is the wheels, with the flying car featuring hubcaps similar to those seen on the Tesla Cybercab and Cybertruck ; the on-stage car featured a set of more intricately styled wheels (pictured above). Take that information and do with it what you will, but Musk promised there will be more live demos in the future, which should provide a better look at the car's capabilities.

To see the spectacle that was the new Tesla Roadster reveal for yourself, you can watch the recorded livestream at the link below.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos’ has invested billions of his fortune into SpaceX rival Blue Origin; documents reveal extraordinary commitment; what Amazon founder said on winners in the space
articles.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has invested a staggering $30 billion of his personal fortune into rocket company Blue Origin since founding it in 2000,
articles.body: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has invested a staggering $30 billion of his personal fortune into rocket company Blue Origin since founding it in 2000, including a fresh $2 billion commitment as the company ramps up efforts to challenge SpaceX's dominance in the commercial space industry, according to a Wall Street Journal report. Documents reviewed by the publication reveal the scale of the Amazon founder's financial backing for Blue Origin, underscoring a long-term commitment that has helped transform the company into a major space player with around 15,000 employees and ambitious growth plans.Jeff Bezos’s $2 billion is part of Blue Origin’s first-ever capital raiseThe latest $2 billion commitment from Bezos forms part of Blue Origin's first-ever fundraising round involving external investors. The company has already secured $10 billion in the oversubscribed financing round, which values the company at approximately $140 billion, according to the report. Bezos, whose net worth stood at about $275 billion in late September according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, has previously sold Amazon shares to help fund Blue Origin's expansion.Revenue targets jump from $800 million to $30 billionThe company is betting heavily on future growth across rocket launches, satellite communications and artificial intelligence infrastructure. Blue Origin generated about $800 million in revenue in 2025, according to the documents cited by the Journal. The company expects revenue to grow to roughly $1.4 billion this year before surging to more than $30 billion by 2030. Part of that projected growth is expected to come from a satellite communications business that has yet to launch hardware into orbit, as well as a planned fleet of AI-focused satellites. Rocket launch services are also expected to contribute significantly to future revenue.Leaner operations under LimpThe company has been sharpening its operations. It carried out a major layoff last year and stopped suborbital tourism flights. Chief Executive Dave Limp, who took the job almost three years ago, has emphasized accelerating missions and technical development, and the company is eager to deliver for customers such as NASA.New Glenn and the SpaceX challengeBlue Origin faces competition across its business lines from other rocket operators and satellite and spacecraft companies, but especially from industry leader SpaceX. According to the documents, Blue Origin expects to narrow SpaceX’s lead with its New Glenn vehicles.New Glenn is a massive rocket with a reusable booster. Blue Origin has flown it on three missions, but it has not flown since a vehicle exploded on a Florida launchpad in May. The company is redeveloping that complex.What Bezos said about winnersBezos said in an interview last year that the space industry has plenty of room for winners. “SpaceX is going to be successful. Blue Origin is going to be successful. And there’s some company out there right now that hasn’t even been founded yet that is also going to be successful,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Britain-sized Doomsday Glacier is melting faster than feared
articles.summary: Antarctica’s ‘Doomsday Glacier’ could unleash a bigger threat than previously feared, with new research warning that it could drive twice as much
articles.body: Antarctica’s ‘Doomsday Glacier’ could unleash a bigger threat than previously feared, with new research warning that it could drive twice as much sea-level rise by 2100 as earlier models predicted.According to CNN, the study found that warm ocean water is penetrating several kilometres beneath Thwaites Glacier, accelerating melting in a zone that conventional ice-sheet models have largely overlooked.Researchers from the University of California, Irvine, and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory said accounting for this process pushed the glacier’s projected contribution to sea-level rise to up to 30 mm by 2100, roughly twice previous estimates.The glacier’s stability could be further threatened if it loses contact with the Mouginot Ridge, an underwater feature that currently helps hold back its retreat.Lead researcher Mattia Poinelli said simulations incorporating a 4–6 kilometre-wide grounding zone indicate a 60 per cent probability of the glacier becoming detached from the ridge by 2100. Co-author Eric Rignot warned that existing projections had struggled to capture the speed of ice loss because key physical processes were missing from earlier models.Thwaites Glacier, which is roughly the size of Britain, is one of Antarctica’s fastest-changing glaciers and a major contributor to global sea-level rise.It has retreated around 25 kilometres in its fastest-flowing western sector since 1996, while its ice loss currently accounts for about 4 per cent of global sea-level rise.According to the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration,if the glacier were to collapse entirely, it could eventually raise global sea levels by around 65 centimetres.Why Thwaites Glacier is shrinkingThe primary driver of Thwaites Glacier’s retreat is relatively warm ocean water melting the ice from below, a process intensified by climate change.Warm, salty water reaches the glacier’s floating ice shelf and grounding zone, where the ice meets the seabed, thinning the ice and weakening the structure that slows the flow of inland ice towards the ocean, according to the British Antarctic Survey.As the glacier thins, its grounding line retreats inland, exposing more ice to seawater. The seabed beneath parts of Thwaites also slopes deeper towards the Antarctic interior, allowing ocean water to penetrate further beneath the ice and potentially accelerate the retreat. NASA research has identified this feedback mechanism as a major reason for concern.How its retreat could affect the climateThe most immediate global consequence would be rising sea levels as more land-based ice flows into the ocean. This would increase the risk of coastal flooding, erosion and storm-surge damage, particularly in low-lying coastal regions.If Thwaites retreats substantially, it could also destabilise neighbouring glaciers, increasing the potential contribution from the wider West Antarctic Ice Sheet.The effects could extend beyond sea levels. Large quantities of freshwater entering the Southern Ocean could alter its salinity and density, potentially affecting ocean circulation and the movement of heat and nutrients.Can cutting emissions slow the Doomsday Glacier’s retreat?Scientists say the most effective way to limit further melting is to rapidly cut greenhouse gas emissions and curb global warming, which is heating the ocean water responsible for melting Thwaites Glacier from below.Reducing emissions from fossil fuels and accelerating the shift to low-carbon energy could limit additional ocean warming and reduce the risk of more severe ice loss.A 2026 study led by the British Antarctic Survey found that Thwaites could continue losing ice for at least 150 years even when ocean-driven melting was switched off in simulations.Researchers say there is no proven intervention that can quickly stop the glacier’s retreat. The priority is to limit further warming while preparing for unavoidable sea-level rise through stronger coastal protection, improved flood planning and restoration of natural barriers such as mangroves.

articles.title: Queensland has acquired parts of three huge cattle properties covering almost 396,000 hectares; the deal protects 174 wetlands on one station and habitat for threatened birds across northern Australia
articles.summary: Queensland has secured major portions of three vast cattle properties across Cape York and the Gulf of Carpentaria, adding almost 396,000 hectares to the
articles.body: Queensland has secured major portions of three vast cattle properties across Cape York and the Gulf of Carpentaria, adding almost 396,000 hectares to the state’s protected area network. The Queensland Government says in a press release that the acquisitions cover 137,000 hectares of Kendall River Station, 90,000 hectares of Westmoreland Station, and 169,000 hectares of Cliffdale Station. The land contains nationally significant wetlands, savanna woodlands, permanent waterholes, and habitat for threatened wildlife, including the palm cockatoo and grey falcon.The deal was delivered through a partnership between the Crisafulli Government and The Nature Conservancy, with the Albanese Government contributing $3.5 million toward Westmoreland Station through its Protecting Important Biodiversity Program. The acquisition is one of the largest recent conservation purchases in northern Australia and is intended to safeguard habitat for future generations. Read more details about it here:Three stations, one conservation goalKendall River Station covers 137,000 hectares and protects important swamp mahogany and Darwin stringybark ecosystems. The Queensland Government says the property also provides habitat for species including the palm cockatoo and white-bellied sea eagle.Westmoreland Station adds another 90,000 hectares and supports threatened wildlife such as the endangered Carpentarian grasswren, grey falcon, and purple-crowned fairywren. These birds depend on intact savanna, riparian zones, and wetland systems, making large-scale habitat protection especially important.Cliffdale Station is the largest of the three acquisitions at 169,000 hectares. It contains 174 wetlands, and 93 percent of the property has been identified as having high or very high aquatic conservation value.Why wetlands matterWetlands are among the most valuable ecosystems in northern Australia. They provide water during dry periods, support fish and invertebrates, filter nutrients, and create feeding and breeding habitat for birds, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals.Cliffdale’s 174 wetlands make it a particularly important addition to Queensland’s conservation estate. The fact that 93 percent of the station has high or very high aquatic conservation value suggests that the property contains an unusually rich network of freshwater habitats. Protecting these systems can also benefit surrounding communities. Healthy wetlands help maintain water quality, reduce the impact of floods, and support the ecological processes that sustain wildlife across the wider landscape.A boost for threatened birdsThe acquisition is especially significant for threatened birds. The palm cockatoo, found in Cape York, relies on mature woodland and nesting hollows, while the grey falcon needs large, undisturbed hunting territories across arid and semi-arid landscapes.Another major beneficiary is the endangered Carpentarian grasswren. The species is endemic to northern Australia and is reliant on specific grassland and savanna habitats, hence large contiguous reserves are critical for its persistence. The purple-crowned fairywren, by contrast, is strongly associated with riparian vegetation along waterways. Protecting permanent waterholes and surrounding habitat can help maintain the conditions this colourful bird needs to breed and persist.A partnership model for conservationThe purchase was made possible through cooperation between government, conservation organisations, and private philanthropy. The Crisafulli Government worked with The Nature Conservancy, while the Albanese Government contributed federal funding to Westmoreland Station.The Nature Conservancy received support from the Wyss Foundation and Holdfast Collective for the purchases. Wyss Foundation President Molly McUsic said the areas are home to numerous threatened birds, wetlands, and other essential habitats.Queensland Environment and Tourism Minister Andrew Powell said, as per the release, that partnerships like this are critical to expanding the state’s protected area estate. He emphasised that national parks should be properly managed while respecting surrounding landholders and communities.Part of a national 30 by 30 targetThe acquisition supports Australia’s commitment to protect 30 percent of its land and oceans by 2030, as per reports. Federal Environment and Water Minister Murray Watt said that Australia has now protected more than 25 percent of its land mass, up from 22 percent in 2022. The federal government’s $3.5 million contribution to Westmoreland Station forms part of its $25 million Protecting Important Biodiversity Areas Program. That programme is designed to help states and territories secure high-value habitat before it is lost or degraded.Queensland’s new acquisitions add a substantial area to that national effort. At almost 396,000 hectares, the combined properties represent a major expansion of protected land in Cape York and the Gulf of Carpentaria.What protection means in practiceAcquiring the land is the first step, but effective conservation will depend on ongoing management. Queensland says it wants national parks to be good neighbours, with practical land management that protects environmental values while considering nearby landholders and communities.Managing fire, invasive species, feral animals, and water quality will be important across such a large landscape. These pressures can affect wetlands, woodland ecosystems and the threatened birds the acquisition is designed to protect. Working in partnership may also help to ensure that conservation does not happen in isolation. Queensland unites government agencies, conservation groups, charitable funders and local communities to manage the land for the benefit of both biodiversity and regional interests.A major win for Northern AustraliaThe acquisition of Kendall River, Westmoreland, and Cliffdale stations represents a significant investment in northern Australia’s natural heritage. It protects wetlands, permanent waterholes, savanna woodlands, and habitat for some of the country’s most distinctive threatened birds.For Queensland, the deal expands the protected area estate by almost 400,000 hectares. For Australia, it strengthens progress toward the 2030 target of protecting 30 percent of land and oceans.Most importantly, it gives species such as the palm cockatoo, grey falcon, Carpentarian grasswren, and purple-crowned fairywren a better chance of surviving in intact, connected habitat. The purchase turns former cattle country into a foundation for long-term conservation across Cape York and the Gulf of Carpentaria.

articles.title: Time is a-changin’: say goodbye to the leap second
articles.summary: Plans to retire it in 2035 are being expedited to prevent potential havoc on tech infrastructure.﻿
articles.body: An important change will soon be made to global timekeeping that aims to prevent potential infrastructure failures akin to the Y2K bug scare. On Thursday, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) voted to scrap the leap second, an ad hoc time adjustment that’s occasionally added so tracked time standards mirror the Earth’s real (and inconsistent) rotation. BIPM members previously agreed in 2022 to cease using leap seconds on or before 2035, but this is now being expedited to take effect on May 20th next year, aligning with World Metrology Day. There’s an unprecedented reason for its retirement being brought forward: changes to the Earth’s rotation may soon require timekeepers to subtract time instead of adding it in order to keep astronomical time in line with atomic time. This has never been attempted before, and there are concerns that doing so could wreak havoc on critical infrastructure that relies on time synchronization. Those fears aren’t unfounded given Foursquare, Reddit, LinkedIn, Yelp, and many other tech platforms have suffered outages in the past when leap seconds have been added. Companies including Meta, Google, Microsoft, and Amazon have all supported efforts to scrap the system. Following the BIPM vote, timekeepers will instead switch to using “leap hours,” allowing atomic and astronomical time to gradually drift apart until an entire hour needs to be added — which isn’t expected to happen for around 3,000 years.

articles.title: A Neanderthal survived a severe facial injury for at least a year before dying 75,000 years ago; a 15mm shoulder-blade hole may be the earliest evidence of lethal violence with a wooden spear
articles.summary: A Neanderthal who lived around 75,000 years ago survived a serious facial injury for at least a year before suffering what researchers believe was a fatal
articles.body: A Neanderthal who lived around 75,000 years ago survived a serious facial injury for at least a year before suffering what researchers believe was a fatal spear wound. The discovery, made at Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, could provide some of the earliest evidence of a deadly attack involving a wooden spear in human evolutionary history.Scientists reached this conclusion after examining the remains of an adult Neanderthal, identified as Shanidar A. A nearly complete left shoulder blade contained a circular hole measuring approximately 15mm across. Researchers believe the shape of the opening is consistent with a sharpened wooden spear passing through the chest and emerging through the bone. They also identified damage to the individual's front teeth, suggesting that the Neanderthal had experienced a separate, serious injury long before death.Although the shoulder wound may have resulted from an attack, scientists have not ruled out a hunting accident. The discovery is particularly important because the same remains offer evidence of both a potentially violent death and survival after an earlier injury that may have required help from other members of the group.Findings of the research led by archaeologists at the University of Cambridge were published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports and shared by Nature.com.What the 15mm hole reveals The shoulder blade was recovered from beneath approximately 7.5 metres of rock and sediment. Despite its age and fragile structure, much of the bone remained intact, allowing scientists to examine the damage in detail.The circular opening, together with small fractures around it, suggested that a pointed object had pierced the bone. Using microscopic examination and micro-computed tomography scans, scientists studied the direction of the impact and fragments found beneath the shoulder blade.The analysis indicates that the weapon entered the front of the body, passed through the left side of the chest and exited through the shoulder blade. Such an injury could have damaged the lungs and major blood vessels, causing death within a short time.The researchers then compared the opening with injuries produced experimentally using prehistoric weapons. Its rounded shape was more consistent with a wooden spear than a stone-tipped weapon, which generally leaves a different pattern of damage.According to Dr Emma Pomeroy, the study's lead author, "Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula," she said as quoted by University of Cambridge.However, the circumstances remain uncertain. A spear used during close-range hunting could have caused the injury accidentally. Researchers also considered deliberate violence because of the wound's position and the force involved.Pomeroy says, "The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal’s body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart."Earlier facial injury and possible careScientists also examined six heavily worn front teeth attributed to Shanidar A, who was estimated to have been around 45 years old at death.One lower incisor had split lengthways, leaving only half the tooth. Nearby teeth had also shifted from their normal positions. Researchers believe the damage was probably caused by a major blow to the mouth or face, although they could not establish whether it resulted from an accident or violence.A thick accumulation of dental calculus, commonly called tartar, had developed over the damaged tooth. This showed that the individual continued living and using the tooth after the injury.According to the researchers, the Neanderthal survived for at least another year, possibly longer. Eating and communicating may have remained difficult during that period. The team believes other Neanderthals may have helped the injured individual survive.Importance of Shanidar Cave According to Reuters, Shanidar Cave, located in the Zagros Mountains of northern Iraq, was used by Neanderthals as a seasonal campsite for tens of thousands of years, Reuters reported. Modern humans, or Homo sapiens, also occupied the cave in a later period. The site overlooks the Great Zab river valley and has been an important source of information about Neanderthals since archaeological excavations began there in the 1950s. Earlier discoveries included remains showing serious disabilities and long-term survival, contributing to research into care within Neanderthal groups.The latest study also examines how the dead were placed inside the cave. Shanidar A was found beneath other Neanderthal remains in a small area measuring approximately 1.5 metres by one metre.The bodies appear to have been deposited at different times, possibly within years or decades of one another. Their repeated placement near a large boulder supports the interpretation that the location was deliberately used for the dead.The researchers also found that a flash flood had disturbed Shanidar A's skeleton after decomposition, explaining why only some bones survived in their original positions.Together, the findings raise questions about Neanderthal social behaviour, including how they treated injured individuals and their dead.The proposed wooden spear injury also adds to evidence that prehistoric humans and their relatives possessed sophisticated woodworking skills. Wooden spears dating back hundreds of thousands of years have previously been discovered in Europe, including at Schoningen in Germany.

articles.title: The incredible flying Tesla Roadster is just for show
articles.summary: The Tesla Roadster drove upside down, flipped over, and flew through the air. But the rocket car wasn’t street legal, or even a real car in the traditional sense.
articles.body: Last night, Elon Musk gave the people what they want: a car driving vertically up a multi-story ramp, launching off the edge, executing a mid-air “kickflip” over a lineup of Teslas, and landing via cold-gas thrusters. That’s what the people want, right? “We were promised flying cars,” sure, but isn’t the operative word in that statement “we”? Because as far as I can tell, everything we saw last night — while extremely cool and incredibly impressive — won’t result in a real, production-ready car you can park, or, I guess, land in your driveway. Tesla’s late-night demonstration in Waco, Texas, certainly gave some corners of the internet what it wants. And the gushing praise and wide-eyed reactions on X, a platform already predisposed to absolving Musk of all his sins, were hard to avoid. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Taken purely as a stunt, the demo was jaw-dropping. Equipping an electric supercar with 600 liters of compressed air, 10 directional cold-gas thruster nozzles, and a 2G suction-fan system directly inspired by SpaceX is undeniably rad. Seeing a 0-to-60 mph launch in under a second pushes the absolute outer limits of physics — even if it could lead to a detached retina or two. Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third-party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition. Tesla says the “Rocket” configuration of the Roadster, the one we saw doing all the cool shit, will be “invite only.” But even that strains credulity. That version of the Roadster removes the passenger seat to make room for the ultra-high-pressure gas tanks, and trades road practicality for short bursts of thruster-powered levitation. But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.” Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance. Tesla skipped basic commercial details like pricing or battery range specs. The Roadster’s range estimate was downgraded from 600 miles to 300 miles. And Musk casually pushed the production window out to 2028 — more than a decade after early adopters handed over $50,000 deposits. Musk himself has acknowledged the Roadster is a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially compared to mass-market models like the Model Y. He also called it “the last best driver’s car,” in a nod to his belief that autonomous driving will define Tesla’s future. Some analysts are already theorizing that the Roadster’s re-release is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger. Musk’s fans on X are practically begging for it — even though it would likely result in the dilution of their own equity. But that’s just table stakes in Musk’s quest to consolidate control of his companies. In some sense, the car had to fly in order to make the preceding decade of missed deadlines feel worth it. Tesla has already been lapped several times in the electric hypercar market. Even some of the Roadster’s most impressive tricks have already been done. There are cars that can drive upside down, cars that can jump in the air, and cars that can accelerate very, very fast. BYD’s Yangwang U9 Extreme uses four electric motors (one more than the Roadster) to produce an insane 3,000 horsepower for a top speed of 308mph in testing — beating Rimac’s Nevera 268mph record. And the McMurtry Spéirling single-seater holds the record for quickest acceleration from 0 to 60 mph in 1.35 seconds. The Roadster could best it, but we’ll need to wait for independent testing to confirm. But no one puts on a show quite like Elon Musk. So if the goal is to score a PR victory, dominate social media feeds, and cement Tesla’s brand as a frontier tech pioneer, then I would say the Roadster demo was a success. Competitors like Rimac, Porsche, and BYD will continue shipping real, track-ready hypercars while Tesla spends another few years refining its rocket-boosted prototype. It’s completely useless as a viable product. But as a 30-minute flex of engineering muscle, it was truly a sight to behold.

articles.title: Tesla's flying Roadster is more fuel for SpaceX merger rumors than a real car
articles.summary: The Roadster showcase was a soft-launch of a merger with SpaceX, of engineering, audacious flair, and Musk's ambitions.
articles.body:
Tesla, strictly speaking, is a car company. But CEO Elon Musk has gone out of his way to tell investors he doesn't want it to be. The adrenaline-soaked Roadster EV unveiling — packed with aerial acrobatics — was another reminder.

Tesla ( TSLA ) was showing off its newest, fastest car. But it was also, in the eyes of many analysts, soft-launching a merger with SpaceX , of engineering, audacious flair, and Musk's ambitions.

The reactions from Tesla's sharpest observers underscored what was left unsaid. "So SpaceX buys Tesla this year. That's has become obvious," wrote Gerber Kawasaki's Ross Gerber, a vocal Tesla shareholder and frequent commentator on Musk's business moves.

The flashy Roadster unveiling placed an exclamation point on simmering chatter about an impending tie-up . Rumors and commentary have been circulating for months, highlighting the shared technology and partnerships that would make for a sensible marriage. Musk himself has heavily hinted at combining his two biggest companies, including on Tesla's latest earnings call. And last month, at the All-In Summit, he emphasized the collaboration between the two.

In a note to clients earlier this month, Barclays analyst Dan Levy said a tie-up "has increasingly become the consensus expectation." The Roadster event — light on details about the actual car business, but heavy on the pizzazz — prompted several other Tesla watchers to hint at or explicitly get behind that forecast.

A note by JPMorgan analysts led by Rajat Gupta pointed to Tesla glossing over what the Roadster means commercially for Tesla, instead showcasing its deep collaboration with SpaceX. Other reactions were more direct.

Gene Munster of Deepwater Management posted his two big takeaways on X , Thursday night. "1. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. 2. Elon can't wait to bring Tesla and SpaceX together."

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said the event strengthened the case for Musk's rocket company and Tesla to operate as one engineering platform. "We believe there is an 80% chance that Tesla and SpaceX merge by the end of 2027 for a number of strategic AI/data driven reasons," he said in a note on Friday.

Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban .

articles.title: Artemis III astronaut talks about ‘honor’ of helping US lead space race
articles.summary: The mission is slated to launch into low Earth orbit in 2027 and will test rendezvous and docking capabilities.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik has expressed the privilege he feels of being part of the Artemis III mission set for 2027.

Artemis III will test lunar landings, though it will not reach the moon. The mission is slated to launch into low Earth orbit in 2027 and will test rendezvous and docking capabilities.

It is seen as a “stepping stone” toward getting boots on the moon again.

“Knowing that (our mission) unlocks the ability for us to land on the moon in 2028,” Bresnik said. “I mean, what an honor, what a pleasure. And the fact that we are accelerating what NASA is doing in space and showing that the country continues to lead in so many areas of space.”

While Artemis II took a trip around the moon, Artemis III is set to perform tests with one or both lunar landers in Earth’s orbit.

The four-person crew will travel to Earth orbit aboard the Orion spacecraft, where they will rendezvous with one or both commercially developed lunar landing systems, which will be launched separately.

Bresnik will command the mission. He is a two-time commander of the International Space Station (ISS). The astronaut joined NASA in 2004 and most recently served as the commander of the ISS for Expedition 53 and flight engineer for Expedition 52.

Bresnik never thought he would grow up to be an astronaut and encouraged others to pursue their dreams.

“The only limits you have are the ones you place on yourself. So don’t let anyone tell you you can’t. And if I had someone telling me that, I would have done things a little differently,” he said.

“Fortunately, I’m where I am, and every step has led me here,” the astronaut added. “But man, I wish I’d had that confidence or that knowledge or somebody, you know, being that supportive back then.”

articles.title: Race to find Amelia Earhart's lost plane hits rough seas as crucial deadline nears
articles.summary: The Purdue University expedition hit severe weather near Nikumaroro, pausing efforts to identify a lagoon object that may be Amelia Earhart's plane.
articles.body: Days into their expedition, the team searching for Amelia Earhart’s missing plane is battling severe weather — and racing to identify a mysterious object that could finally solve the aviator's disappearance. Purdue University announced in a Thursday update that the 17-person expedition was forced to pause field operations after winds and rough seas made it too dangerous to reach Nikumaroro by transport boat. The group is investigating the Taraia Object, a visual anomaly in the island's lagoon that researchers believe could be the wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E. GIANT MEAT-EATING CRABS WITH CRUSHING GRIP COMPLICATE AMELIA EARHART EXPEDITION ON REMOTE ISLAND Winds and rough seas near Nikumaroro "made conditions unsafe," Purdue University said. "Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned — and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected — before the team must depart the atoll and return to Tarawa, Kiribati," the university said. Because Nikumaroro is 17 hours ahead of Eastern time in the United States, an update could come as early as Saturday, although Purdue did not give a specific release time. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER UNEXPECTED TWIST IN SHIPWRECK MYSTERY AFTER CLUES DON'T ADD UP The university also said the team had begun collecting data on the Taraia Object, but it cautioned that it was too early to draw conclusions. "We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience," Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute and a leader of the expedition, said in a statement. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "This is a complex scientific process," he added. "You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyze it and reach sound conclusions." Earhart disappeared on July 2, 1937 while attempting to become the first woman to fly around the world. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS She and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished during one of the final legs of their journey after departing Lae, New Guinea, for Howland Island. Earhart was just 39 years old when she vanished — one of the most famous people in the world at the time. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Purdue became involved in the latest search in February 2025, when expedition leader Rick Pettigrew approached the Purdue Research Foundation about investigating the Taraia Object. Purdue spokesperson Trevor Peters previously told Fox News Digital that, if the Taraia Object is Earhart's airplane, the team hopes to conduct a full-scale archaeological excavation next year with the proper permissions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The eventual curation of the wreckage has been the subject of discussions with [the Republic of] Kiribati, and although nothing has been finalized, ALI [the Archaeological Legacy Institute] and the Purdue Research Foundation share a dream of returning the plane to Purdue to be displayed, consistent with Amelia's original wishes," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine advances in occupied Donetsk as Trump hands Putin diesel deal
articles.summary: Ukraine’s ‘Operation Vivaldi’ reclaimed more occupied territory in Donetsk during a week when Trump sided with Russia.
articles.body:
The United States’s relationship with Ukraine came under extraordinary strain during the past week, as US President Donald Trump lifted some oil sanctions against Russia and was feared to have restricted Ukraine’s access to US intelligence and satellite services, hobbling its defences.

“It is a pity we are losing … a strong partner,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalist Piers Morgan, speaking of the US.

“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said. “This is not [the] right side of history.”

Trump on October 9 invited Russia to sell 1.8 million tonnes of diesel to the global market by the end of the year, to help bring down transport prices.

That effectively reversed the Lindsey Graham Act, which Trump had signed into law days earlier. The law gave him the ability to punish countries buying Russian oil with secondary sanctions.

Ukraine’s partners did not share intelligence that five ballistic missiles were headed towards Kyiv on October 13, Zelenskyy said, without naming the US. Those missiles struck Kyiv’s Thermal Power Plant number 4, one of the capital’s biggest, resulting in power outages.

Russia then pounded Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure on October 14, when Ukraine reported it had restricted use of SpaceX’s satellite navigation services, which it uses to defend itself.

Over a 24-hour period, Russia launched 850 drones and 39 missiles, striking 30 energy targets across 19 regions of Ukraine, despite the fact that Trump had declared an energy ceasefire on October 11.

“This level of blatant disregard for the United States by Russia has not been seen before,” Zelenskyy said.

Starshield, the military element of the Starlink satellite network owned by SpaceX, capped Ukraine’s use of its navigation services at 160 km/h (100mph).

This meant that Ukraine lost sight of its interceptors above that speed, making it difficult or impossible to stop Russian jet-powered Geran-4 drones, which fly at speeds exceeding 500 km/h (310mph).

Six in 10 Russian drones are now jet-powered, Zelenskyy said.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” wrote SpaceX owner Elon Musk.

Starshield services had begun to return to normal on October 15, sources at Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said.

Ukraine is so heavily targeted by Russian aerial strikes that an outage in its ability to navigate interceptors for a prolonged period could be ruinous.

During September, its air force intercepted more than 4,700 drones and missiles of various kinds.

Starshield is equally important for Ukraine’s ability to hobble Russian offensive operations. Ukraine has wrought havoc with Russian supply lines for months, striking fuel trucks, bridges, ammunition warehouses and air defences.

During September alone, Ukraine’s military said it had struck 40 command posts and 50 logistics facilities.

The Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine’s data showed that strikes fell from a daily average of 2,300 to 1,678 on October 14 and 1,053 on October 15.

This was not the first such disruption of services under the Trump administration.

The US had also stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine in March, helping Russia reclaim its Kursk region, which Ukraine had counter-invaded.

Despite the setbacks this week, Ukraine has continued to win back territory.

Its Third Army Corps concluded a fourth phase of Operation Vivaldi in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, reclaiming an additional 100sq km of territory (40sq miles), said Corps commander Andrii Biletskyi.

That brought the operation’s gains to 275sq km (100sq miles) and 16 settlements since August, and brought Russia’s overall gains this year close to nil.

The campaign was designed to push back against a Russian effort to seize the town of Lyman. A separate counteroffensive further south pushed back against an attempted Russian takeover of Dobropillya. Ukraine saw the two initiatives as an effort to surround the “fortress cities” of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk in a pincer movement.

Ukraine’s counteroffensives have drawn away Russian units directly facing Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, paralysing this part of the front.

“Russian forces averaged around 14 attacks per day in the Sloviansk direction in August 2026, five in September 2026, and three per day thus far in October 2026,” wrote the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank.

“Russian forces averaged around three attacks per day in the Kramatorsk direction in August 2026, one in September 2026, and only an average of 0.3 thus far in October 2026,” the ISW said.

“We are stopping all enemy attempts to advance or infiltrate,” said Zelenskyy. “Ukraine’s positions on the front remain strong, and this year they are the strongest they have been in a long time.”

Zelenskyy said Russian forces outnumber Ukraine’s by six to eight times in parts of the front, and it appeared that they have recently received reinforcements.

Robert Brovdi, the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine, said the personnel increase “translates into a significant increase” in Russian casualties.

During the first two weeks of October, Brovdi said, Russian casualties increased by 25 percent compared with the first two weeks in September and by almost 60 percent compared with the first two weeks in August.

In Dobropyllia, the Russian casualties were higher than anywhere else on the front, he said, 43 percent above September’s rate and double the rate in August.

Ukraine’s success is due in part to its production of domestically designed drones in partnership with European allies.

Ukraine’s Defence Ministry’s orders in 2026 were higher by half than in 2025, it said, and delivery volumes were almost four times what they had been last year.

While Ukraine respected Trump’s energy ceasefire for three days, it returned to striking Russian refineries on October 15.

It also continued to strike non-energy targets throughout the week.

Ukraine struck a facility manufacturing explosives and rocket fuel in Nizhny Novgorod on October 9, and a plant making additives for missile fuels in the Tver region.

On October 15, it destroyed four Sukhoi fighters and damaged another two at the Borisoglebsk airfield in the Voronezh region.

Ukraine also targeted three data centres owned by the Russian cloud services company Yandex, destroying or crippling those in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir between October 8 and 11. It also struck a data centre owned by Sberbank on October 14.

The strikes caused Russians to lose online payment and other services.
